title: The great commandment
hookLine: love God, love your neighbor: all of it in two lines
tomorrow: how can anyone call people who mourn "blessed"?

cards: It's the kind of question that goes around a comment thread: if you could keep just one rule, which one? In Matthew it's asked out loud, as a test, with people watching for a slip.
An expert in the law puts it to Jesus: "Master, which is the great commandment in the law?" There are plenty to choose from. Everyone leans in to hear which one he'll pick.

teach.b: He doesn't pick one. He picks two, and both come out of scripture his listeners already knew.

"Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself."
The first comes from Deuteronomy, right after the words Hear, O Israel, which Deuteronomy says to talk of when you lie down and when you rise up.
Jews still pray those words, the Shema: shared ground at the very root of this answer.
The second comes from Leviticus, from a chapter of everyday rules about leaving some harvest for the poor, paying wages on time, and never tripping up the blind.
One to tell a friend tonight: "love thy neighbour as thyself" was scripture before Jesus quoted it. He sets the two side by side and says the second is like the first.

Love for God and love for the person next to you aren't two projects. They're one love, facing two ways. Then the line that names this day: "On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets."
Hang, like a door on two hinges.
Take either one away and the door falls. Churches work out the details differently. The hinges stay the same.

how: Some churches read Jesus's summary of the law aloud near the start of worship, and Christians learn the two commandments in Sunday school and catechism as a summary of how to live.

o: honor your father and your mother above all
never work on the Sabbath, whatever happens
love God, and love your neighbor as yourself

games.q: the great commandment — tap the pairs.
p: hang all the law and the prophets

s: 'love thy neighbour as thyself' was first said by Jesus
it's from Leviticus 19:18; Jesus quotes scripture his listeners already knew.
asked for the one great commandment, Jesus gives two
love God, and the second 'is like unto it': love your neighbor.
the Shema, 'Hear, O Israel,' belongs only to the past
Jews still pray those words; Jesus's first commandment comes right after them.

games.q: your coworker says, "loving God is church stuff. loving people is the real work." what does Jesus's answer do with that?
o: agrees: the second commandment matters more.
joins them: the second is like the first, and everything hangs on both.
pushes back: love God first, and people can wait.
games.why: Matthew 22:39–40: 'the second is like unto it,' and on these two hang all the law and the prophets. one love, facing two ways.

practice: Close your eyes and hold two faces in mind. First, turn toward God with one honest line of love or thanks, or toward whatever you hold most dear.
Then turn toward one neighbor you'll see soon, and wish them, by name, the good you'd want for yourself.

wordCard.voice: The great commandment. Love God with all you are, and your neighbor as yourself: two lines from the Hebrew Scriptures, with everything hanging on them.

orig.note: Greek: thou shalt love, the verb that opens both commandments in Matthew 22:37 and 22:39.

carryVoice: Keep this: on these two, two hinges and one door that swings on both. Day done.
